claim: siRNA depletion of DAXX in ATRX-KO cells significantly decreased the expression of gB transcripts during productive ICP0-null HSV infection.
source: Here we report that siRNA depletion of DAXX in ATRX-KO cells significantly decreased the expression of gB transcripts during productive ICP0-null HSV infection.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Similar dual anti-viral and pro-viral effects have recently been reported for PML.
source: Similar dual anti-viral and pro-viral effects have recently been reported for PML (Newhart et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016), and the H3.3-specific chaperone, HIRA, has been shown to both enhance and restrict viral infection depending on context (Placek et al., 2009; Rai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The H3.3-specific chaperone, HIRA, has been shown to both enhance and restrict viral infection depending on context.
source: Similar dual anti-viral and pro-viral effects have recently been reported for PML (Newhart et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016), and the H3.3-specific chaperone, HIRA, has been shown to both enhance and restrict viral infection depending on context (Placek et al., 2009; Rai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DAXX is restrictive while in complex with ATRX but at a later stage of infection, after dispersion of PML-NBs and degradation of ATRX, DAXX may promote HSV gene expression or replication.
source: It is possible that DAXX is restrictive while in complex with ATRX but at a later stage of infection, after dispersion of PML-NBs and degradation of ATRX, DAXX may promote HSV gene expression or replication.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the dual effects of DAXX observed in the experiments.

claim: DAXX has ATRX-independent functions that may have important implications for viral restriction, cancer biology, and epigenetics.
source: Our results contribute to a growing body of literature that is revealing ATRX-independent functions of DAXX that may have important implications for viral restriction, cancer biology, and epigenetics (He et al., 2015; Hoelper et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and the authors' own findings.

claim: ATRX restricts viral infection by maintaining viral heterochromatin stability, resulting in DNA that is less accessible to transcription and viral replication factors.
source: We hypothesize that ATRX restricts viral infection by maintaining viral heterochromatin stability, resulting in DNA that is less accessible to transcription and viral replication factors (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed effects of ATRX on viral chromatin and gene expression.

claim: Decreased histone retention or histone reloading in the absence of ATRX/DAXX could explain the observed loss of H3 and H3K9me3 on HSV genomes, elevated levels of viral transcription, and the enhanced accumulation of nascent viral DNA.
source: Though de novo formation of HSV-associated heterochromatin was unaffected by the absence of ATRX (Figure 9B), decreased histone retention or histone reloading in the absence of ATRX/DAXX could conceivably explain the observed loss of H3 and H3K9me3 on HSV genomes, elevated levels of viral transcription, and the enhanced accumulation of nascent viral DNA that we observed by 8 hpi in ATRX-KO cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Decreased histone retention may lead to increased histone dynamics, reduced nucleosome density, and transiently expose transcription factor binding sites, resulting in elevated transcription.
source: Decreased histone retention may lead to increased histone dynamics, reduced nucleosome density, and transiently expose transcription factor binding sites, resulting in elevated transcription (Huang and Zhu, 2014) and increased accessibility for viral replication factors.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When viral DNA synthesis was blocked with PAA, HSV DNA in Control cells continued to accumulate H3 and H3K9me3 from 4 to 8 hpi.
source: When viral DNA synthesis was blocked with PAA, HSV DNA in Control cells continued to accumulate H3 and H3K9me3 from 4 to 8 hpi.
evidence: This is an observation from the ChIP-qPCR experiments with PAA treatment shown in Figure 6.

claim: In ATRX-KO cells, HSV DNA-associated H3 and H3K9me3 did not accumulate significantly from 4-8hpi when viral DNA synthesis was blocked with PAA.
source: In contrast, HSV DNA-associated H3 and H3K9me3 did not accumulate significantly in ATRX-KO cells from 4-8hpi, suggesting that in the absence of ATRX, histone exchange rates had reached an equilibrium by 4 hpi.
evidence: This is an observation from the ChIP-qPCR experiments with PAA treatment shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of ATRX, histone exchange rates had reached an equilibrium by 4 hpi.
source: In contrast, HSV DNA-associated H3 and H3K9me3 did not accumulate significantly in ATRX-KO cells from 4-8hpi, suggesting that in the absence of ATRX, histone exchange rates had reached an equilibrium by 4 hpi.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ChIP-qPCR data with PAA treatment.

claim: The model that best fits the observations is one in which ATRX promotes heterochromatin accumulation by mediating modified histone retention.
source: While there may be more than one way to explain these observations, we think the model that best fits these observations is one in which ATRX promotes heterochromatin accumulation by mediating modified histone retention.
evidence: This is the authors' preferred mechanistic model based on their experimental observations.

claim: ATRX is known to be recruited to heterochromatin through the interaction of its ADD domain with the H3K9me3 histone tail modification.
source: ATRX is known to be recruited to heterochromatin through the interaction of its ADD domain with the H3K9me3 histone tail modification (Iwase et al., 2011), and is known to be required for both H3.3 and H3K9me3 maintenance on regions of cellular DNA (Lewis et al., 2010; Sadic et al., 2015; He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ATRX is known to be required for both H3.3 and H3K9me3 maintenance on regions of cellular DNA.
source: ATRX is known to be recruited to heterochromatin through the interaction of its ADD domain with the H3K9me3 histone tail modification (Iwase et al., 2011), and is known to be required for both H3.3 and H3K9me3 maintenance on regions of cellular DNA (Lewis et al., 2010; Sadic et al., 2015; He et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ATRX can be recruited by direct interaction with heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1).
source: It can also be recruited by direct interaction with heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) (Eustermann et al., 2011; Bérubé et al., 2000), a chromatin remodeling factor which has been reported to localize to HSV gene promoters during infection (Ferenczy and DeLuca, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HP1 has been reported to localize to HSV gene promoters during infection.
source: It can also be recruited by direct interaction with heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) (Eustermann et al., 2011; Bérubé et al., 2000), a chromatin remodeling factor which has been reported to localize to HSV gene promoters during infection (Ferenczy and DeLuca, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ATRX may act to recruit DAXX to viral DNA through its interaction with H3K9me3 or HP1 and promote rapid replacement of histones that dissociate from viral DNA.
source: ATRX may act to recruit DAXX to viral DNA through its interaction with H3K9me3 or HP1 and promote rapid replacement of histones that dissociate from viral DNA (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Replaced histones could be rapidly modified with H3K9me3 by histone lysine methyltransferases SUV39H1 or SETDB1 that are known to be recruited by HP1.
source: These histones could then be rapidly modified with H3K9me3 by histone lysine methyltransferases SUV39H1 or SETDB1 that are known to be recruited by HP1, thus maintaining heterochromatin composition and density on the HSV DNA.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis that incorporates established knowledge about HP1-recruited methyltransferases.

claim: The model is likely relevant to the maintenance of DNA virus latency.
source: Our model is also likely relevant to the maintenance of DNA virus latency.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to viral latency.

claim: The EBV protein BNRF1 has been shown to bind to DAXX and separate it from the ATRX/DAXX complex.
source: The EBV protein BNRF1 has been shown to bind to DAXX and separate it from the ATRX/DAXX complex (Tsai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Depletion of DAXX or ATRX led to EBV reactivation in lymphoblastoid cells.
source: That study also showed that depletion of DAXX or ATRX led to EBV reactivation in lymphoblastoid cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (referring to the Tsai et al., 2011 study).

claim: Through its interaction with DAXX, BNRF1 was shown to promote increased mobilization and turnover of H3.3 during FRAP experiments.
source: Through its interaction with DAXX, BNRF1 was shown to promote increased mobilization and turnover of H3.3 during FRAP experiments (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The observed increase in H3.3 turnover has been proposed to facilitate expression of viral latent genes and the establishment of latent EBV infection.
source: The observed increase in H3.3 turnover has been proposed to facilitate expression of viral latent genes and the establishment of latent EBV infection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from published literature about the mechanism of EBV latency establishment.

claim: ATRX and DAXX have been detected localizing to viral genomes in neurons of mice latently infected with HSV-1.
source: ATRX and DAXX have also been detected localizing to viral genomes in neurons of mice latently infected with HSV-1 (63).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (though the citation format appears incomplete).

claim: The ATRX/DAXX mechanism may be important for both lytic and latent DNA virus infections.
source: These reports are consistent with our model that ATRX/DAXX promotes heterochromatin integrity to enhance epigenetic silencing of viral genes and proposes that this mechanism may be important for both lytic and latent DNA virus infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion that extends the findings to both lytic and latent infections based on the authors' data and published literature.

claim: Transcription by RNA Pol II evicts histones which are then quickly replaced.
source: Transcription by RNA Pol II evicts histones which are then quickly replaced (Schwabish and Struhl, 2004) by the FACT complex, which has been implicated in both the disassembly and reassembly of histone components during transcription (Belotserkovskaya et al., 2003; Mason and Struhl, 2003; Xin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The FACT complex has been implicated in both the disassembly and reassembly of histone components during transcription.
source: Transcription by RNA Pol II evicts histones which are then quickly replaced (Schwabish and Struhl, 2004) by the FACT complex, which has been implicated in both the disassembly and reassembly of histone components during transcription (Belotserkovskaya et al., 2003; Mason and Struhl, 2003; Xin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: As the level of transcription increases in the absence of ATRX, the equilibrium between eviction and deposition could shift in favor of eviction and result in an apparent reduction in H3.3 and H3K9me3.
source: Based on our observations of viral chromatin and viral gene expression in the absence of ATRX, we expect that as the level of transcription increases in the absence of ATRX, the equilibrium between eviction and deposition could shift in favor of eviction and result in an apparent reduction in H3.3 and H3K9me3.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: ATRX has been shown to be required to silence transcription of an eGFP-retrotransposon reporter in response to continuous dox-induced transcription.
source: Supporting this idea, ATRX has been shown to be required to silence transcription of an eGFP-retrotransposon reporter in response to continuous dox-induced transcription (Sadic et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In the Sadic et al. study, ATRX depletion had minor effects on the initial establishment of H3K9me3 at the reporter element, but it was required for the efficient re-establishment of H3K9me3 after transcriptional challenge was ended.
source: In that study, ATRX depletion had minor effects on the initial establishment of H3K9me3 at the reporter element, but it was required for the efficient re-establishment of H3K9me3 after transcriptional challenge was ended.
evidence: This is a description of findings from published literature.

claim: ATRX protected against expression of minor satellite sequences in mouse embryonic stem cell derived neurons upon neuronal stimulation.
source: Similarly, ATRX protected against expression of minor satellite sequences in mouse embryonic stem cell derived neurons upon neuronal stimulation (Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PML was recently reported to influence ATRX/DAXX complex activity.
source: PML was recently reported to influence ATRX/DAXX complex activity and loss of PML may increase H3.3 turnover at PML-associated domains (PADS) (Delbarre et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of PML may increase H3.3 turnover at PML-associated domains (PADS).
source: PML was recently reported to influence ATRX/DAXX complex activity and loss of PML may increase H3.3 turnover at PML-associated domains (PADS) (Delbarre et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ATRX is required for heterochromatin maintenance at both pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres.
source: Because ATRX is required for heterochromatin maintenance at both pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres (Lewis et al., 2010; Goldberg et al., 2010; McDowell et al., 1999), it is not surprising that pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres have both been shown to exhibit high levels of chromatin stability with very low histone turnover (Kraushaar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres have both been shown to exhibit high levels of chromatin stability with very low histone turnover.
source: Because ATRX is required for heterochromatin maintenance at both pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres (Lewis et al., 2010; Goldberg et al., 2010; McDowell et al., 1999), it is not surprising that pericentric heterochromatin and telomeres have both been shown to exhibit high levels of chromatin stability with very low histone turnover (Kraushaar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A major function of ATRX in heterochromatin maintenance is in stabilizing chromatin density and promoting histone retention.
source: Consequently, we suggest that a major function of ATRX in heterochromatin maintenance is in stabilizing chromatin density and promoting histone retention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and published literature on ATRX function.

claim: ATRX could be promoting the re-establishment of heterochromatin in the wake of RNA Pol II mediated transcription, perhaps in a fashion similar to the FACT-complex.
source: However, increased histone retention is not the only possible mechanism of action. ATRX could also be promoting the re-establishment of heterochromatin in the wake of RNA Pol II mediated transcription, perhaps in a fashion similar to the FACT-complex.
evidence: This is an alternative mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: ATRX could be stabilizing chromatin by inhibiting transcription or replication through a DNA damage pathway.
source: Likewise, ATRX could be stabilizing chromatin by inhibiting transcription or replication through a DNA damage pathway.
evidence: This is another alternative mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: There are at least two stages of epigenetic regulation involved in restriction of viral gene expression: 1. Initial loading of heterochromatin; 2. Maintenance of heterochromatin during chromatin stress.
source: Our finding that ATRX restricts HSV gene expression by promoting the maintenance of viral heterochromatin raises the idea that there are at least two stages of epigenetic regulation involved in restriction of viral gene expression: 1. Initial loading of heterochromatin; 2. Maintenance of heterochromatin during chromatin stress, such as transcription and replication.
evidence: This is a major conceptual conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Before this report, the formation of viral chromatin and the maintenance of viral chromatin were not understood to be separate mechanisms.
source: Although viral chromatin structure is known to be dynamic (Gibeault et al., 2016), before this report, the formation of viral chromatin and the maintenance of viral chromatin were not understood to be separate mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: DNA viruses have evolved specific mechanisms for dismantling or disabling the ATRX/DAXX pathway rather than blocking the initial formation of heterochromatin.
source: Importantly, DNA viruses have evolved specific mechanisms for dismantling or disabling the ATRX/DAXX pathway rather than blocking the initial formation of heterochromatin.
evidence: This is an observation about viral evolution strategies based on published literature and the authors' findings.

claim: There may be some role for the early formation of chromatin in the viral life cycle.
source: This argues there may be some role for the early formation of chromatin in the viral life cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the observation that viruses target maintenance rather than formation.

claim: HIRA and ASF1A promote histone occupation on HSV DNA during the first few hours of infection but do not appear to be restrictive during this same period of time.
source: This is supported by reports that HIRA and ASF1A promote histone occupation on HSV DNA during the first few hours of infection but do not appear to be restrictive during this same period of time (Oh et al., 2012; Placek et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The heterochromatin maintenance mechanism mediated by ATRX appears to act as a critical restrictive hurdle to productive infection.
source: Conversely, the heterochromatin maintenance mechanism mediated by ATRX appears to act as a critical restrictive hurdle to productive infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the restrictive effects of ATRX on viral gene expression and replication.

claim: The roles of chromatin factors in epigenetically silencing viral DNA may reflect their functions in cellular chromatin assembly and maintenance.
source: The multiple stages of epigenetic restriction of viral genomes uncovered here involve cellular chromatin factors. Therefore, their roles in epigenetically silencing viral DNA may reflect their functions in cellular chromatin assembly and maintenance.
evidence: This is a general inference about the relationship between viral and cellular chromatin regulation.

claim: Cellular chromatin structure must be maintained during transcription, DNA synthesis, and mitosis.
source: Cellular chromatin structure must be maintained during transcription, DNA synthesis, and mitosis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about cellular chromatin biology.

claim: Multiple mechanisms likely exist to deal with each of the chromatin stressors (transcription, DNA synthesis, and mitosis).
source: Thus, it is likely that multiple mechanisms exist to deal with each of these chromatin stressors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the complexity of chromatin regulation.

claim: The stages of viral epigenetic regulation by the host cell as defined here will serve to identify host epigenetic factors that may function in similar host cell pathways.
source: The stages of viral epigenetic regulation by the host cell as defined here will serve to identify host epigenetic factors that may function in similar host cell pathways, and this knowledge could provide insights critical to the development of epigenetic therapies for both viral and host diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader impact and applications of the findings.

claim: This knowledge could provide insights critical to the development of epigenetic therapies for both viral and host diseases.
source: The stages of viral epigenetic regulation by the host cell as defined here will serve to identify host epigenetic factors that may function in similar host cell pathways, and this knowledge could provide insights critical to the development of epigenetic therapies for both viral and host diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential translational applications of the findings.
